content: Quartz is the most abundant mineral found in the Earth's continental crust, although feldspar is more common globally. It is composed of a lattice of silica (silicon and oxygen) tetrahedra. Quartz has a hardness of 7 on the Mohs scale and a density of 2.65 g/cm³. Quartz belongs to the rhombohedral crystal system. Its ideal crystal form is a six-sided prism that terminates with six-sided pyramids at each end. However, in nature, quartz crystals are often twinned, distorted, or intergrown with other quartz crystals or minerals, which can obscure their ideal shape. In some cases, they lack distinct crystal faces and appear massive. Well-formed quartz crystals typically grow in a bed, where they extend freely into a void. However, because they are attached to a matrix at one end, only one termination pyramid is usually present. Quartz geodes are an example of this, where the void is roughly spherical and lined with inward-pointing crystals. Pure quartz is either colorless or white, but it can occur in various colored forms, such as rose quartz, amethyst, smoky quartz, and milky quartz. Quartz varieties are classified into two main categories: macrocrystalline (individual crystals visible to the naked eye) and microcrystalline or cryptocrystalline (aggregates of crystals visible only under magnification). Chalcedony is a general term for cryptocrystalline quartz. Cryptocrystalline varieties are typically translucent or opaque, while macrocrystalline varieties are usually transparent. Historically, quartz varieties were named based on their color, but modern scientific classification focuses on their microstructure. For cryptocrystalline quartz, color is a secondary identifier, whereas for macrocrystalline quartz, it is a primary identifier. Not all quartz varieties occur naturally. For example, prasiolite, an olive-green quartz, is often produced by heat treatment, although natural prasiolite has been found in Lower Silesia, Poland. Similarly, most citrine is created by heat-treating amethyst, and carnelian is often heat-treated to enhance its color. Due to the frequent twinning of natural quartz, much of the quartz used in industrial applications is synthesized. Large, flawless, untwinned quartz crystals are produced in autoclaves using the hydrothermal process, which is also used to synthesize emeralds. While these synthetic materials are commonly referred to as quartz, the correct term for them is silicon dioxide. Quartz is commonly found in hydrothermal veins and pegmatites. Well-formed quartz crystals can grow to several meters in length and weigh hundreds of kilograms. These veins may also contain precious metals like gold or silver, making them valuable for mining. Erosion of pegmatites can expose large pockets of quartz crystals, sometimes referred to as cathedrals. Quartz is also a common component of granite, sandstone, limestone, and many other igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks. Quartz has several related silica minerals. Tridymite and cristobalite are high-temperature polymorphs of SiO₂ found in high-silica volcanic rocks. Lechatelierite is an amorphous silica glass formed when lightning strikes quartz sand. The name quartz is derived from the German word Quarz, which has Slavic origins. In Czech, miners referred to it as křemen. Some sources suggest the name comes from the Saxon term Querkluftertz, meaning cross-vein ore. Quartz has been associated with mystical properties in various cultures. For example, it is identified as the substance maban in Australian Aboriginal mythology and is often found in burial contexts in European passage tombs, such as Newgrange and Carrowmore in Ireland. The Irish term for quartz, grian cloch, translates to stone of the sun. The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder believed quartz to be permanently frozen water ice, a theory he supported by noting its presence near glaciers in the Alps but not on volcanic mountains. He also observed that large quartz crystals were shaped into spheres to cool the hands and that quartz could split light into a spectrum. This belief persisted until the 1600s. Nicolas Steno's work on quartz laid the foundation for modern crystallography, as he discovered that the long prism faces of quartz crystals always form a perfect 60-degree angle, regardless of distortion. In the 20th century, Charles Sawyer developed the commercial process for manufacturing quartz crystals in Cleveland, Ohio, transitioning from mined quartz to synthetic quartz for use in electrical devices. Quartz's piezoelectric properties were discovered by Jacques and Pierre Curie in 1880. These properties allow quartz to generate an electric charge when subjected to mechanical stress. Walter Guyton Cady developed the first quartz oscillator in 1921, and George Washington Pierce patented quartz crystal oscillators in 1923. Warren Marrison created the first quartz oscillator clock in 1927, based on the work of Cady and Pierce. Quartz crystals are rotary polar, meaning they can rotate the plane of polarization of light passing through them. When an alternating electric current is applied, quartz crystals vibrate. Quartz's piezoelectric properties have been utilized in various technologies. For example, early phonograph pickups used quartz crystals. Today, one of the most common applications is in quartz crystal oscillators, such as those found in quartz clocks.
